title: Sociological, Political & Theological Emergence in Colony Simulations

core_principles: Citizens have distinct physiological, psychological, and social needs (Hunger, Exhaustion, Spiritual Devotion, Safety, Kinship).
Unmet needs generate individual stress and grievances; aggregated grievances across demographics produce collective unrest and political pressure.
Authority figures (guards, magistrates, inquisitors) are subjected to the same need and loyalty equations as common citizens.
modules.operational_rule: Never spawn artificial guard enforcement when civic authority is bankrupt; guards must draw wages, consume food, and evaluate personal loyalty.

core_principles: Power resides in competing interest groups: The Clerisy (Theology), The Guilds (Capital), The Laborers (Production), and The Guard (Coercion).
Regime legitimacy is mathematically computed from faction appeasement, treasury reserves, and food security.
Edicts (such as Curfew, Grain Requisitions, or Tithe Exemptions) shift faction loyalty vectors and can provoke strikes or rebellions.
modules.operational_rule: Civic edicts like curfew must be toggleable political states governed by regime legitimacy and civil unrest.

core_principles: Religion is a social technology that modulates citizen morale, obedience, and tolerance for hardship.
Prolonged economic strain causes theological schisms: citizens abandon orthodox cathedral rites in favor of underground heretical cults.
Heretical movements can form clandestine mutual-aid networks that organize strikes or smuggle supplies past authorities.
modules.operational_rule: Model religious fervor as a dynamic variable that can either stabilize civic authority or spark ideological revolutions.
